name: Ngundi
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Winkhart, Benedikt. 2025. A comparative sketch of Ngundi. In Ines Fiedler & Lee J. Pratchett (eds.), Areas, families, and pools aplenty: a Festschrift for Tom Güldemann, 341-351. Berlin: Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin. DOI 10.18452/32606 (open access,https://edoc.hu-berlin.de/18452/33224).
catalog_locator: Sec. 2.2 'Tone', p. 343; sec. 2.3 'Phonotactics', p. 343; Table 6, p. 350.
catalog_quote: Like all known Mundu-Baka members, Ngundi is a tone language. It features three lexical register tones, namely high (H), mid (M), and low (L). High tone is marked by ´, low tone by `, whilst mid tone is diacritically unmarked. [...] Contour tones occur only on long vowels or diphthongs, suggesting the mora as the tone-bearing unit. VV-sequences and thus contour tones are scarce. [...] Ngundi features four syllable types of which CV is the most frequent. The types CV1V2 and CV1V1 are rarer and the latter often occurs as a fast speech variant of CV1.LV1 verbs. Initial V is very rare. Closed syllables do not exist.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

At the stated locator, sec. 2.2 'Tone' on printed p. 343 (p. 3), the text reads exactly: 'Like all known Mundu-Baka members, Ngundi is a tone language. It features three lexical register tones, namely high (H), mid (M), and low (L). High tone is marked by ´, low tone by `, whilst mid tone is diacritically unmarked.' followed after ex. (2) by 'Contour tones occur only on long vowels or diphthongs, suggesting the mora as the tone-bearing unit. VV-sequences and thus contour tones are scarce.'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ngundi is described as a three-level register-tone language (H/M/L, mora as TBU); the only existing description says nothing about word stress or accent, so no stress rule can be stated.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical tone on (mostly CV) syllables/morae; word shapes CV to CV.CV.CV(.CV). No statement about word- or phrase-level prominence.
new_statements.identity_note: Winkhart 2025 describes Ngundi (ISO gdi, glottocode gund1247), the Ubangi/Mundu-Baka language closely related to Baka and Limassa, from ca. 25 speakers at Seke and Thanry (Likouala, Rep. Congo). His fn. 1 warns it is NOT the Bantu C10 language Ngundi [ndn] spoken in the same area; older sources (Ouzilleau 1911) call it 'Gundi (sur la Bodingue)'. The single Glottolog 5.1 'grammar sketch' ref (Balep, 'bakaa') is a computerized mis-assignment and not about this language.
